Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in unauthorized creation, deletion or modification of critical data on Oracle Access Manager versions 12.2.1.4.0 and 14.1.2.1.0. The last “perfect 10” vulnerability in Oracle’s latest report is in the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne Orchestrator product of Oracle JD Edwards, tracked as CVE-2026-91299 . title: Dual BIOS: The laptop security feature SMBs don’t know they need
raw_text: Every security checklist starts with the basics: strong passwords, multifactor authentication, spotting phishing, and keeping software up to date. All four protect what happens after a laptop starts. But some attackers are more focused on what happens before. That’s the domain of the BIOS, the first code that runs when a laptop powers on. It checks the hardware, then hands control to the operating system. Malware planted at this level can load before the operating system does, so it can evade antivirus tools and even survive a drive wipe or reinstall. For small and midsize businesses (SMBs), the cost of an incident goes beyond the bill to fix it. It’s also about the work that stops in the meantime. The Verizon Business 2026 Breach Impact Study (which analyzes cyber insurance claims), found that SMBs suffered losses accounting for up to 7% of their total revenue. It also identified business interruption as the fastest growing source of loss. Detection isn’t recovery Modern laptops verify their firmware before booting, so a tampered BIOS image usually fails, though attackers are increasingly exploiting flaws that enable them to slip past those checks. But even a failed attack can do damage, because a BIOS that doesn’t pass verification can leave the laptop unable to boot. Of course, not every BIOS failure is malicious. An update that’s interrupted, such as a laptop losing power before it finishes, gives the same result. Either way, a corrupted BIOS effectively bricks the device. IT must spend time and money restoring or replacing it, and in the meantime, a remote employee can lose days of work waiting for a replacement. What’s more, if the failure was the result of a cyberattack, the business may need to reset credentials and possibly notify customers. How a dual BIOS provides a second chance The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) frames firmware security around 3 goals: protect firmware from unauthorized changes, detect unauthorized changes, and recover quickly and securely. Recovery is the part that keeps employees working. Some laptop manufacturers are now providing SMBs with an effective defense against compromised or corrupted firmware. A dual BIOS, sometimes called a dual ROM design, puts two firmware chips on the motherboard. The first holds the system BIOS, while the second stores a protected copy. In this way, if the primary BIOS becomes corrupted, the laptop can fail over to the backup, and employees can get back to work almost immediately. That’s because recovery doesn’t require a network connection or a call to the help desk. Firmware resilience for small teams Dual BIOS designs have long been common in servers, where staying available is critical, as well as in gaming PCs and higher-end enterprise machines, but few small businesses think to look for this capability. However, with so many employees working remotely and with attackers increasingly targeting firmware, a dual BIOS is rapidly becoming a necessary security capability for an SMB laptop. The ASUS ExpertBook A7 brings dual BIOS protection to small-business laptops. If the laptop detects a BIOS integrity failure during startup, recovery begins automatically. The event is also recorded in the BIOS System Event Log, so IT can confirm what happened, and the log can flag signs of physical tampering, such as the laptop’s case being opened. The ExpertBook A7 is also powered by up to an Intel ® Core™ 7 Series 3 processor to keep multitasking, communication, browsing, and content creation moving smoothly throughout the workday. SMB laptops don’t need to be vulnerable to firmware attacks or corruption. A dual BIOS deserves a place on every SMB’s list of required laptop features. Learn more about the ASUS ExpertBook A7.
summary: Every security checklist starts with the basics: strong passwords, multifactor authentication, spotting phishing, and keeping software up to date. All four protect what happens after a laptop starts. But some attackers are more focused on what happens before. That’s the domain of the BIOS, the first code that runs when a laptop powers on.

title: Meta hit with $25 billion fine for illegally sharing user data
raw_text: A judge in New Mexico has fined Meta $25 billion for its flouting of data privacy laws between 2010 and 2021, including its controversial passing of data to Cambridge Analytica . The action serves as a stark reminder to enterprises not to play fast and loose with data protection legislation, as the consequences could be highly damaging. Meta faced the court action after it was revealed that data company Cambridge Analytica had improperly obtained personal data that Facebook was holding. It could have been even worse for Meta. Under New Mexico law, the damages could have been as high as $219 billion , which would have exceeded its revenue for 2025. Judge Francis Mathew reduced his demand to $25 billion without explanation, but was scathing in his judgment on the social media company. “The harm in this matter is difficult to overstate, and goes to the heart of Facebook’s basic business proposition,” he wrote in his order . The company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws and had deceived its users by giving third-party app developers access to personal information without consent. The company is set to appeal against the judgment. It’s been a bad couple of months for Meta. In August, the company agreed to an $18 billion settlement over claims that Facebook and Instagram failed to prevent children from accessing its platforms. And in July, another judge in New Mexico fined the company just under $1 billion for, again, failing to protect minors. In Europe, companies are also under pressure over data protection. Last year, breaches of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) rose 22% , with a record €1.2 billion in fines issued, as legislators look to get tougher on big tech companies. title: eMudhra quits global TLS certificate market after compromise of CA signing keys
raw_text: Indian digital trust company eMudhra has announced that it is exiting the global SSL/TLS certificate business and is offering customers certificates issued by Sectigo as an alternative, following the compromise of private keys behind eight of its intermediate certificate authorities. The company’s board decided “to voluntarily withdraw from the global SSL/TLS certificate business,” eMudhra said in a press note . It added that data sovereignty and compliance requirements had increased the business’s complexity and cost. “The level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” eMudhra Chairman V Srinivasan said in the announcement. The company said it will contact affected customers to replace certificates free of cost. It also said it will keep revocation and certificate status services running until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced. Sectigo offered as an alternative In the customer update, eMudhra said it is making Sectigo-issued certificates available to all its customers. “Our G1 root certificates remain active and continue to be fully supported,” the company said in the update. The October 22 release said the G1 RSA roots “will continue to serve customers until this transition is complete.” eMudhra said it would provide replacement certificates free of charge through its partners and continue operating revocation and certificate-status services until all certificates it issued had expired or been replaced. CertiNext users can request Sectigo certificates through their accounts; other customers can contact eMudhra support, the statement added. Niyati Daftary, principal analyst at Gartner, said organizations should view the G1 roots “as a possible bridge, not automatically as the final destination.” “With the company exiting global SSL/TLS and its remaining roots still subject to browser scrutiny, the prudent course is to move critical services to an independent, fully trusted CA wherever the deadline allows,” Daftary said. If G1 is used to prevent an immediate outage, she recommended setting a firm deadline and documenting a subsequent migration plan. She recommended including issuing authorities, intermediate and root certificates, cross-signing arrangements, revocation infrastructure, and browser trust status in third-party risk assessments. Yash Kadakia, co-founder and CTO of Security Brigade, said that moving to another root operated by the same company does not necessarily address concerns over trust and governance. “The last thing organisations need is to migrate twice,” Kadakia said. Sectigo did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Java and other systems may need separate fixes Replacing a website’s certificate may not address every dependency in an enterprise environment, according to Sakshi Grover, research director at IDC. She said residual exposure lies in systems that maintain their own trust stores and do not update on the same schedule as browsers. These include Java keystores, language runtimes, container images, mutual TLS configurations, proxies, load balancers, VPN and security appliances, and embedded devices. “The harder finding for many organizations will be that they can’t answer these questions at all,” Grover said, referring to where certificate trust decisions are made outside browsers and operating systems. Grover noted that Google reported finding no certificates chaining to the affected intermediates in Certificate Transparency logs before they were blocked. She said that was reassuring for clients that enforce Certificate Transparency, but some non-browser applications and devices do not. Exploitation would also require an attacker to be positioned to intercept traffic, she said, describing the remaining risk as limited and targeted rather than broad. Azul, a Java vendor, said in a statement that Java does not check certificate revocation by default. An unpatched Java Development Kit (JDK) could therefore continue to accept a forged certificate signed with a compromised intermediate key if the relevant chain remains trusted. Azul said it released updated Azul Zulu Builds of OpenJDK and Azul Prime. The updates add the eight affected certificates to the JDK’s blocked-certificate list, the company said. Grover recommended that security teams first identify where trust decisions occur outside browsers and operating systems, prioritising systems that accept connections from external parties and mutual TLS endpoints. Teams should then determine which systems can be updated to distrust a specific intermediate certificate or public key, she said. Chrome deadline for certificate holders Mozilla has removed emSign ECC Root CA – G3, the root that signed the eight compromised intermediates , from its trust store. Google said in a blog post that the root’s removal from the Chrome Root Store is expected to reach all devices on the morning of October 27, Pacific time. “To avoid breakage, website operators with certificates chaining to emSign ECC Root CA – G3 must immediately acquire and install a new TLS certificate,” Google said in the post. Daftary said enterprises often know their certificate reseller but not the CA hierarchy underpinning their trust. “That creates an unrecognized fourth-party risk capable of affecting thousands of services at once,” she said. She added that CISOs should include issuing CAs, roots, cross-signing arrangements, and revocation infrastructure in their third-party cyber risk assessments. “You can outsource a service, but you cannot outsource accountability,” Kadakia said. It added that data sovereignty and compliance requirements had increased the business’s complexity and cost. “The level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” eMudhra Chairman V Srinivasan said in the announcement.

title: The ‘Mythos moment’ has already passed. Now comes the hard part for cybersecurity
raw_text: When Anthropic introduced Claude Mythos Preview, the cybersecurity debate quickly turned to what AI could do: uncover decades-old vulnerabilities, develop working exploits and accelerate tasks that once required specialist expertise . Anthropic noted that Mythos discovered software flaws no human had caught, and early tests showed it could carry out multi-stage network attacks in minutes, tasks that once took skilled pen testers days. Security leaders and cyber defenders let out an initial sigh of relief when it was announced that Mythos would be available to a select few, with an extension to 150 other organizations. The Mythos moment and hype have now passed, and the harder task is turning its warning into practical defensive readiness. In other words, the “ Mythos moment” and the initial “shock” is over. Now comes the hard part: can organizations identify their exposures, prioritize real risks and patch or mitigate them fast enough to stay ahead of AI-powered attacks? Can they be as fast as AI in even discovering them to begin with? AI-accelerated attacks are already here to stay There is no hiding from it now; AI-enabled and accelerated attacks are here already, and they are already rewriting cyber-attack playbooks worldwide. In 2026, Stanford’s AI Index reports that AI agents now solve cybersecurity problems 93% of the time, up from just 15% in 2024. Independent tests confirm this trend: the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) found Claude Mythos Preview could autonomously execute a 32-step simulated corporate network attack (a scenario that humans would take ~20 hours to complete) and retrieve flags hidden on target machines. In short, frontier AI models can chain together reconnaissance, exploitation and privilege escalation without human help. In these trials, Mythos reliably discovered and exploited vulnerabilities autonomously, tasks that would take human professionals days of work. Allied research backs this up. A Cloud Security Alliance report notes that attackers now operate at machine speed, whereas defenders still often operate on “organizational speed.” In practice, this means patch cycles of weeks or months no longer keep pace with exploit windows measured in hours. Widely deployed software (operating systems, browsers, network devices, etc.) – precisely the high-impact targets many enterprises depend on are now rapidly weaponized. Email is also not spared as attackers have now stepped up how they leverage AI-enabled prompt injection phishing attacks to deceive employees into wiring money to fake accounts, Vulnerabilities and exploits are exploding in growth Data shows this isn’t a theoretical worry: the volume of known flaws and their exploitation is surging. Google’s Threat Intelligence group found that reported vulnerabilities doubled from January to July 2026 (rising from ~5,000 to over 10,000 per month ). At the same time, the number of those vulnerabilities actually exploited in the wild nearly doubled, from an average of ~10.5 per month in 2025 to ~18 per month in early 2026. Even zero-day (previously unknown) exploits ticked up slightly. Google and others warn that this trend will continue. If rapid AI-assisted discovery and exploitation keep accelerating, defenders cannot afford “unprioritized mass-patching” as in the past. Instead, they must move to a threat-intelligence-driven triage model: focus on the vulnerabilities actually being targeted, and automate as much response as possible. This means continuous scanning, asset inventory and risk-based prioritization — often called exposure management using tools like Wiz, Tenable and Microsoft Defender for Cloud. For example, Security Boulevard explains that an exposure management program uses AI to constantly map assets, vulnerabilities and misconfigurations , then automatically prioritize and remediate the riskiest ones. This approach is essentially a “Mythos-ready” security program — one designed to handle the avalanche of findings that AI will generate, and to fix them at machine speed. AI, essentially battling AI Using AI defensively Importantly, defenders can use AI as well as attackers, so it benefits both sides of the coin. Anthropic’s own Project Glasswing is a case in point, as seen earlier. In early April 2026, only ~50 organizations were testing Mythos Preview, but within weeks they had already run it across their codebases and uncovered over 10,000 high- or critical-severity flaw s. Anthropic is now expanding Glasswing to ~150 additional organizations deemed critical (power, healthcare, communications, etc.) whose code impacts millions of users. The aim is to train industry on new AI-powered workflows: Partners share best practices, triage vulnerabilities together and even use AI to suggest fixes and pre-emptively harden code. Glasswing’s lessons show that AI can speed up defensive tasks too. For example, Mythos-level models can be repurposed to write patches or convert legacy code into memory-safe languages, and to run “AI red teams” against one’s own systems. Anthropic reports that partners are now using Mythos to automatically generate fixes, and their new public tool (Claude Security) helps scan code and suggest patches using a slightly safer variant of Mythos. In practice, organizations should consider adding AI to their security toolchain and leverage automated penetration testing, intelligent asset discovery and tagging, and AI-assisted patch generation to help keep pace with attackers. Reinforce the fundamentals Even as we deploy sophisticated tools, the basics still matter more than ever. AISI emphasizes that Mythos’s impact actually highlights the importance of cybersecurity basics — regular patching, strong access controls, secure configurations and comprehensive logging, just as is seen in the UK’s Cyber Essentials. In other words, if attackers can automate exploits, defenders must double down on hygiene and detection. With exploit windows collapsing to hours, organizations may need to accelerate patch cycles. This might mean more frequent updates, rolling hotfixes, or virtual patching via network controls when immediate fixes aren’t available. Least privilege and segmentation also must be in place to reduce each user or system’s access to only what it needs. An attacker (or malicious AI agent) with stolen credentials should find it hard to move laterally or escalate privileges. Network segmentation and micro-segmentation can slow or isolate attacks even if they penetrate the perimeter. Incident response rehearsals should also update playbooks to account for fast, AI-enabled attacks. For example, test scenarios where key accounts or credentials are compromised and ensure “break-glass” administrative accounts or recovery keys are secured (offline if possible) so you can take back control even if your primary identity provider or domain is down. In short, building resilience means blending new AI-driven practices with solid engineering. As Anthropic warns, Mythos-class capabilities are coming to many organizations soon and with fewer safeguards than the preview had. There is also no saying if China will get their hands on something similar and make it open source, which means attackers will also gain access to it. Security teams must adapt now by working at machine speed: automate exposure discovery and patching, enforce strict access controls, and enhance detection and response. Only by assuming that some attacks will succeed can organizations design defenses that contain the damage. The Mythos moment, when powerful AI grabbed headlines, has indeed passed and what matters now is translating its warning into practical readiness. The AI genie is out of the bottle, and cyber attackers will leverage these tools at the same time as we also tell it our security wishes.

title: The AI notetaker risk is now an everywhere problem
raw_text: The businesspeople adopting AI notetakers are not being reckless. They are responding to a real business need. Our teams are in meetings all day with companies we support, and the idea that we could read a clean summary of every one of them at the end of the day makes us better partners to our customers. At the AI-first startups we spend time with, a new account manager can walk in on day one, inherit the full recorded history of every customer conversation, and ask the AI what that customer actually cares about. That is not surveillance culture for its own sake. It’s a better way to serve people. Still, AI notetakers present cyber risks , as we have been warning about for the past year: shadow adoption measured in hundreds of accounts in a matter of weeks, vendors without SOC 2 or real encryption, consent liability, litigation exposure. In April, one of us stood on stage at the [un]prompted conference and argued that the most important attendee in your meetings is no longer a person. AI notetakers decide what matters, assigning the action items and providing the summary that becomes the meeting’s official record. But our early warnings about AI notetakers shared an assumption we no longer hold: that the notetaker joins the meeting. That assumption quietly died this summer, as the notetaker has left the meeting platform and moved onto the body — and policies haven’t noticed let alone caught up to this change yet. From the meeting to the wrist On July 28, Granola, the AI notetaker we see most often in our worlds, launched an Apple Watch app . One tap on the wrist and it records whatever happens around you. No bot joining the call, no banner announcing itself, no laptop open on the table. The same week, DEF CON banned Meta-style smart glasses from the conference floor over recording concerns. Meta, meanwhile, had already acquired Limitless , the AI pendant company, folding always-on personal recording into the largest consumer hardware pipeline in the world. One public company we’ve worked with now screens attendees for smart glasses before all-hands meetings where unreleased plans are discussed. We’ve tested this ourselves, putting the watch under a jacket sleeve, tapping once, and recording an entire evening walk. Clean transcript. Nobody could have known. In the United States, recording someone without their permission depends on which state you are standing in. California says you can’t, but many states say you can. More importantly we still have no norms of disclosure, and the hardware is now designed to be invisible. The record is not neutral Since the April talk , we have met a steady stream of people telling us how they game these systems. One person described doing prompt injection against a notetaker in a live meeting, right as we walked offstage. Another explained the simplest trick we have heard: join early, and for the five minutes you are alone with the notetakers, calmly narrate the outcomes you want captured as the most important takeaways. A third said he figured out how to silently crash other companies’ notetakers, so the meeting ends and there is no record. There is academic research behind all this. Call it manipulation or call it strategic communication. The methods work. Notetaking systems also fail on their own. We have watched a transcript mishear one word, then reinterpret the rest of the conversation to fit the error. Colleagues with accents the models handle poorly carry more of that risk than the rest of us. And these tools are no longer stenographers. They have memories. Granola pulls context from prior meetings and background on the people in the meeting into today’s meeting notes. That is useful, but it also means a summary shared outside your company could leak reasoning from meetings the other party was never in. Then there is the case that should be on every policy writer’s mind. Last November, a Campbell’s security executive was terminated for what they said during a meeting secretly recorded by an employee during what he thought was a private lunch conversation. The recording surfaced months later through an employment lawyer, and the executive was gone within days. Whatever you think of what was said, notice the mechanism: no notetaker bot, no meeting platform. One person, one device, one conversation the speaker believed was off the record. There is no such thing anymore. What a serious policy looks like Boards and legal teams are now asking their CISOs for notetaker policies. Having helped several organizations think through this, here is where we land. Transparency always. If a recording tool is running, everyone present knows. The lightest version we recommend: Change your display name to “Name + AI notetaker.” And the rule must bind employees, too. An employee who records a colleague without disclosure is committing a fireable offense, full stop, before we ever discuss what the recording contains. Classify your meetings. At one firm, we wrote a formal policy naming which meetings may never be recorded. Yours might include M&A, legal, HR, and board executive sessions. Decide deliberately, in writing, before the tools decide for you. Govern other people’s notetakers. When an auditor walks into your building, their laptop has to meet your standards. Apply the same principle to recording. If another organization records your employees, you should know, and you should get a copy. Choose your retention posture. A full transcript is a different corporate record than a summary. Decide whether transcripts are destroyed by default, with legal holds as the exception, or kept forever. Do not let the vendor’s default decide. Treat notetaker vendors like what they are: startups holding your most sensitive conversations in their cloud. Vendor security review, data-reuse terms, indemnification language. Brewer v. Otter.ai , a class action alleging Otter’s notetaker recorded meetings without everyone’s consent and used the recordings to train models, and the sudden shutdown of Novacy both happened for a reason. Assign a human. Every transcript that becomes a record needs a named owner responsible for reviewing its accuracy, no matter whose tool recorded the call. Remember that some may train employees to steer the transcript, the way a lawyer protects the record in a deposition. We understand the instinct, and reviewing the record for accuracy is exactly right. An organization that quietly optimizes its official records has bigger problems coming. We used to debate whether to let the notetaker into the meeting. That debate is over, because the meeting is now everywhere the recorder goes. Write your policies for the world where the microphone is already in the room, because it is.

title: Microsoft Frontier Tour London: Agentic AI governance in the spotlight
raw_text:
During the opening keynote at the company’s Frontier Tour event in London, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella discussed how the company would be addressing the growing concern of tokenomics.

Analyst Gartner has predicted that by 2030, a failure to adopt adaptive artificial intelligence (AI) governance runtime controls will triple the cost of AI deployments, eroding value. It warned that standard cloud billing alerts are a lagging indicator of overspending.

In its Cost governance is a non-negotiable addition to AI governance report, Gartner said: “Relying on these escalations hours or days after overspending has been identified delays mitigation and fails to prevent immediate curtailing of runaway inference costs at runtime.”

Discussing how Microsoft would be tackling potential runaway costs associated with overuse of AI inference, Nadella spoke about a Microsoft project that provides AI model orchestration, enabling organisations to select a model, either run locally or in the public cloud.

“We now have HydraFusion, which is a learned model where you are now able to take advantage of powerful local models or an RTX Spark,” he said. “You now have very capable coding models. You can start using HyperFusion whenever a task or one of the sub-agents of a task can be done and can be satisfied by using just a local model.”

According to Nadella, this means IT departments can essentially provide “an infinite token factory”.

The company made Project HydraFusion available on GitHub in September as a research preview. The project’s goal is to deliver what Microsoft describes as “frontier intelligence through runtime orchestration”. In the GitHub post, Microsoft said HydraFusion creates a full execution plan, choosing from models across multiple providers to draft, critique and revise, or cascade to more powerful models to complete a task.

Nadella said that when an AI agent uses an AI model, it is necessary to log its chain of thought in a human-readable form. This log needs to show that the agent has complied with the organisation’s governance and compliance rules. Given that multiple AI agents may be required to complete a task, each one needs to be uniquely identifiable.

Nadella also discussed how Microsoft Agent 365 provides the agentic AI control plane for IT operations teams. He said Agent 365 “holds every agent identified, and manages and governs their policies”. According to Nadella, it also supports security operations and the budgeting requirements for FinOps.

He described how AI agents could work internally in an enterprise, where some work as penetration testers to attack enterprise IT systems, while others are tasked with fixing the security holes identified.

“You now have red agents that are continuously simulating the attacks, and you have blue agents that are continuously defending,” said Nadella. “Then you have green agents that are continuously remediating the vulnerabilities they find.”

Analyst Gartner has predicted that by 2030, a failure to adopt adaptive artificial intelligence (AI) governance runtime controls will triple the cost of AI deployments, eroding value. It warned that standard cloud billing alerts are a lagging indicator of overspending.

In its Cost governance is a non-negotiable addition to AI governance report, Gartner said: “Relying on these escalations hours or days after overspending has been identified delays mitigation and fails to prevent immediate curtailing of runaway inference costs at runtime.”

Discussing how Microsoft would be tackling potential runaway costs associated with overuse of AI inference, Nadella spoke about a Microsoft project that provides AI model orchestration, enabling organisations to select a model, either run locally or in the public cloud.

“We now have HydraFusion, which is a learned model where you are now able to take advantage of powerful local models or an RTX Spark,” he said. “You now have very capable coding models. According to Nadella, this means IT departments can essentially provide “an infinite token factory”.

title: Can Britain’s grid keep up with the datacentre boom?
raw_text:
Ramping datacentre demand is putting a new kind of pressure on the UK’s energy grid. Developers are jostling for position in an increasingly saturated connection queue as new facility plans arrive faster than the network that must accommodate them can grow.

Supporting this wave of infrastructure requires major investment in cabling, substations and transmission capacity. In August, for example, the National Grid announced its North West London Upgrade, a £1bn project that will connect five new datacentres across Bedfordshire, Hertfordshire and London, with 1GW of electricity demand.

That project illustrates a wider shift across the country. As digital demand grows, the financial pressure to connect new infrastructure is felt by developers – and potentially by consumers too – while the need for new substations, cables and transmission capacity looks likely to reshape Britain’s digital geography as it pushes datacentre development to locations where power is available.

In this article, we look at whether Britain’s grid can keep up with the datacentre boom. We examine the sheer scale of the transmission and substation build now required, the speculative connection queue that is pushing developers north, and the increasingly urgent question of who pays for it all – the developers racing to connect, or the households whose bills ultimately fund the network.

Anatomy of a £1bn grid upgrade

The North West London Upgrade shows just how much physical infrastructure is needed to accommodate new datacentre facilities.

The project will see the installation of around 60km of new high-voltage cable, 35km of re-cabling between Sundon and Elstree, and upgrades to more than 200km of overhead lines. At Elstree, the agency is also extending an existing 400kV substation, and building a new 132kV substation at Letchmore Heath to connect the new datacentres.

The upgrade is only one part of a much bigger programme of investment in Britain’s electricity network. Ofgem’s RIIO-3 price control, for example, includes up to £10.7bn for electricity transmission between 2026 and 2031, with flexible mechanisms potentially taking investment to as much as £90bn as projects mature.

Elisabeth Cremona, energy infrastructure lead at energy think tank Ember, tells Computer Weekly that the scale of investment is a response to the unprecedented speed at which these new facilities come online.

“Datacentres represent a huge load,” she says. “You’re essentially looking at putting 500,000 houses on the grid in a single location really, really fast, and that’s just never happened before. Households don’t come online that fast, factories don’t come online that fast.”

Typically, says Cremona, building out or upgrading a grid takes between five and 15 years, while a datacentre can be ready to come online in 18 months. Bringing datacentres online quickly is also fast becoming a competitive advantage for businesses.

“Developers are behaving differently to any previous class of large energy user,” she says. “Rather than wait patiently in established queues, they’re moving to find loopholes, to find a place where they can connect immediately.”

For years, the UK’s datacentre industry has been heavily concentrated around London and the M4 corridor, driven by proximity to customers, existing fibre networks, established datacentre ecosystems and access to major business markets.

Now, with increased onus on speedy connection times and a backlog of connection requests, projects are shifting north.

Analysis of data from construction project information provider Barbour ABI finds that of the UK’s top 10 datacentre projects, only one – at East Havering in Essex – is in the London area. The remainder, totalling just under 4GW, are spread north from Oxfordshire to Lincolnshire, North Wales, the north-east and Scotland.

A changing grid landscape

According to Ofgem, connection offers rose from 41GW to 125GW between November 2024 and June 2025, with datacentres accounting for at least 80GW of that demand. Connection wait times have stretched as a result, some by as much as 15 years.

Part of the backlog is self-inflicted. Developers, aware of how slow the process is, submit multiple speculative applications for the same site to see which clears first, and that creates “zombie applications”.

Ofgem has proposed reforms intended to remove speculative and non-viable projects from the queue. Large datacentre developers would have to pay an upfront commitment fee when accepting a connection offer, which would range from £237,500 to £712,500 per megawatt. The fee would be refunded when a project reaches energisation but forfeited if it leaves the queue early.

Developers would also have to demonstrate that projects are commercially and technically ready to progress.

Matt Salter, global head of datacentres at Onnec, says the proposals reflect how tight the market has become.

“Ofgem’s ‘Pay to Stay’ proposals are a sign of just how tight the UK’s datacentre power market has become,” he tells Computer Weekly. “Asking developers to prove projects are real and ready to move makes sense, but it adds another pressure point for operators already being pushed to build faster.”

Research by Onnec shows that 92% of operators are compressing build timelines to keep pace with artificial intelligence (AI) demand, while 75% say speed-to-market pressure is forcing design decisions before infrastructure requirements are fully understood.

Salter says this creates the risk of adding to grid capacity without properly coordinating it with the rest of a facility’s infrastructure.

“The £1bn National Grid upgrade shows just how much investment is now needed, but more grid capacity on its own will not fix this,” he says. “Power, cooling, cabling and compute need to be planned together from day one, or we risk spending billions connecting new datacentres only to spend more fixing them after go-live.”

The issue is not unique to Britain. In March, Denmark’s grid operator suspended new connection requests after receiving roughly 60GW of applications in a country whose peak demand is around 7GW.

An increasingly common response to lengthening connection times is for developers to simply move where there is capacity.

Follow the power: One operator’s move north

For Spencer Lamb, CEO of datacentre operator Kao Data, the shift described above is already shaping investment decisions.

“Grid availability is one of the most important factors in determining when and where new datacentres are built,” he tells Computer Weekly. “If you cannot secure power within a commercially viable timeframe, it becomes extremely difficult to justify investing in a location, regardless of its other advantages.”

As a result, he says, operators are increasingly choosing sites where capacity already exists rather than waiting years for network upgrades. It is one reason Kao Data is investing £450m in a new facility in Greater Manchester. Lamb says the city region offered tech and AI research heritage, government support, a brownfield site that could be redeveloped for the benefit of the community, and a realistic timeline for power delivery.

He cautioned against reading the National Grid’s North West London Upgrade purely as a response to AI. Some substations, he says, have been in planning for many years, driven by demand for cloud, enterprise computing and digital services.

“What AI has done is accelerate the conversation and intensify pressures,” he says. “The reality is that the UK’s electricity infrastructure has been under increasing strain for some time, and significant long-term investment will be required if the country wants to maintain its position as a leading destination for datacentre and AI investment.”

Who pays for the new infrastructure?

While developers do bear some of the cost of these new infrastructure buildouts, the costs of expanding the grid are ultimately recovered through regulated network charges paid by households and businesses. So, the question of who pays for new infrastructure is increasingly significant for the public as power demand ramps up.

An Ofgem spokesperson tells Computer Weekly it is alert to the risk that “consumers should not unfairly shoulder the costs of connecting” datacentres, and that its bid to clean up the connection queue aims to mitigate this risk.

The regulator’s Demand Connections Reform programme is also designed to reduce the likelihood of consumers funding infrastructure that is ultimately not needed because projects fail to progress.

“Our recent consultation will help shape reforms that will help to ensure viable projects, including datacentres, connect faster and network costs are shared fairly,” says the spokesperson.

Concentration of datacentres also matters, with location materially affecting network costs, reinforcement requirements and connection timescales.

“If you suddenly get a massive cluster of datacentres,” says Ember’s Cremona, “the system operator has to build out a huge amount of transmission lines, substations, and all these very, very expensive things to supply them with power.”

With developers pushed to areas of less concentrated connection, she warns they run the risk of prioritising speed over everything else – including cost for businesses and consumers. Additionally, datacentres rarely draw as much power as they request, meaning bills could rise by more than the actual load justifies.

“They operate on average at around 50%,” says Cremona. “So that means you build a huge amount of transmission infrastructure, and they only use half of it. They’re not even using it fully, and you’re billed in a way that isn’t the most cost-efficient.”

Managing datacentre buildout is therefore a necessity in terms of not overwhelming the grid and in keeping costs down for the public. One solution is to make datacentre demand more flexible, though this remains a difficult pill to swallow for operators facing consumer demand for always-on cloud and enterprise workloads. Cremona says it’s still something worth aiming for, though the road to get there may be long.

“If you could enforce flexibility, developers would get online faster and you would bring down network requirements,” she says. “It’s really a win-win for everyone.”

Can the grid keep up with AI?

Britain’s datacentre ambitions are increasingly becoming an electricity infrastructure problem. The North West London Upgrade demonstrates the physical scale of investment required to connect just five datacentre facilities, while the wider connection queue shows how quickly demand is outstripping available capacity.

Asked whether the UK is doing enough to keep power availability in step with planned capacity, Kao Data’s Lamb is blunt: “In short, no.”

Too often, he says, discussions focus on securing capacity in a handful of established markets, rather than taking a more strategic view of where power is available today and how future demand can be distributed across the country.

“The remaining bottleneck is therefore not simply generation capacity itself, but the speed, transparency and coordination needed to connect demand with available power,” he says. “We need to deliver new network upgrades before the UK’s AI and economic opportunity is lost.”
